title: Analysis of regulating ecosystem services at the mediterranean nature reserve of Castelporziano (Rome, Italy) in response to changing environmental conditions
abstract: Abstract The Castelporziano Presidential Estate, a State Nature Reserve of roughly 6,000 hectares covered by natural forests, with over 30 years of field data collection is a precious data hub that might contribute to better understand the effects of Climate Change abiotic and biotic-related stress on natural vegetation and, eventually, to their ecosystem services provision. This research presents on-going studies on plant-environment interactions conducted within the Estate, with a focus on ecosystem carbon fluxes, pollution (ozone and particulate matter), drought and heat stress, and biotic infections that have occurred over time. The present study concentrates over the period from 2013 to 2024. In the first part, we present a series of continuous measurements on a semi-hourly basis, which was undertaken to build up a time series capable of interpreting the effect of the control factors (climate, ecological processes, water availability) on the eco-physiological parameters of the holm oak forest. Ten years of high-frequency measurements allowed us to estimate the possible effect of climate and water availability on carbon assimilation. The holm oak forest of Castelporziano showed high rates of carbon assimilation each year with minimal changes in response to drought and high temperatures, thus making this ecosystem particularly resilient to climate changes. In the second part, we present remote sensing-based analyses that investigate changes of vegetation health and function over the last six years, which were affected by both biotic (pest invasion) and abiotic (more frequent and intense droughts) factors.
field: Ecosystem services in response to environmental change
problem: The paper addresses the challenge of assessing how Mediterranean forest ecosystems respond to escalating, combined abiotic (drought, heat) and biotic (pest invasions) stressors from climate change, which threaten their resilience and capacity to provide crucial regulating services like carbon sequestration and air pollution removal.
method: This study combines a ten-year analysis of high-frequency eddy covariance measurements of carbon fluxes with a six-year remote sensing analysis of vegetation health to assess a Mediterranean forest's response to environmental changes, including drought, heat stress, pollution, and biotic infections.
task: The task is to analyze the regulating ecosystem services of the Castelporziano nature reserve in response to changing environmental conditions, such as climate change, pollution, drought, and biotic infections, using long-term field data and remote sensing.
innovation: This study integrates a decade of ecosystem-level carbon flux measurements with satellite-based vegetation monitoring to demonstrate the high drought resilience of holm oak forests compared to the severe degradation of pine forests from pest attacks within the Castelporziano Nature Reserve.

The Presidential Estate of Castelporziano (CPE) is a State Nature Reserve of 6,000 hectares covered by natural and planted forests (Manes et al. 2021; Conte et al. 2022). The Presidential Estate of Castelporziano (CPE) is a State Nature Reserve of 6,000 hectares covered by natural and planted forests (Manes et al. 2021; Conte et al. 2022). The climate is strictly Mediterranean: with average monthly summer and winter temperatures reaching 25 °C and 6–12 °C and mean annual precipitation equal to 731 mm (Fig. 1), with a marked period of aridity in July-August (Manes et al. 1997a; Seufert et al. 1997). From a meteorological and geographical point of view, the CPE can be considered fully representative of the coastal areas of the Mediterranean basin as it is located near the sea, at the entrance to Tiber Valley, with the volcanic complex of Albano Hills (i.e. Castelli Romani) 20 km NE from the Reserve.

Carbon and water vapour flux measurements were performed using the Eddy Covariance technique (Fares et al. 2014), which involves rapid and continuous measurements (10 Hz – 10 measurements per second), on the top of the experimental tower, of water and CO2 concentrations using an infrared gas analyzer (LI-7200, Lincoln, NE, USA) co-located with a sonic anemometer (Gill Windmaster Pro in use until 2018, then replaced with Gill HS-50) used to measure instantaneously the wind speed and direction while the signals were recorded using a data logger (CR3000, Campbell Scientific, Shepshed, UK).

Finally, the most striking negative change of NDVI pertains to the pine forest (see Fig. 5; Table 3) that underwent a strong infestation of Tomicus destruens W. and Toumeyella parvicornis in the last six to seven years, that eventually brought most of the pine forest to death.

Therefore, it should be considered that the stress factors for the vegetation of Castelporziano are represented by both abiotic stress (climate changes and air pollution first and foremost), and biotic stresses that, especially in the last decade, are threatening the health of ecosystems and the provision of crucial ecosystem services by the Estate for the benefit of the metropolitan Rome area.
